paper_title: StyleStream 2.0: Fast and Controllable Streaming Voice Style Conversion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Voice style conversion (VSC) aims to transform a source utterance to match the timbre, accent, and emotion of a target voice while preserving linguistic content. StyleStream 1.0 introduced the first streamable zero-shot VSC system with state-of-the-art conversion quality, but remained limited in two ways: approximately 1s end-to-end latency on consumer hardware, and the lack of a text-based interface for designing or editing target voices. We present StyleStream 2.0, a fast and controllable streaming VSC framework that addresses these limitations. To reduce latency, we train a few-step pixel MeanFlow model and further fine-tune it with autoregressive feedback inspired by Self Forcing, improving robustness under streaming inference. This reduces end-to-end latency to 520~ms on a consumer GPU, a 2x speedup over StyleStream 1.0, while maintaining conversion quality. To enable controllable style manipulation, we remove the mel-spectrogram context and instead route target style information through a compact style embedding. In this embedding space, we train a unified text-conditioned flow matching model that supports both text-based voice design, which maps natural language prompts to voice styles, and instruction-based voice editing, which modifies a specific attribute of a source utterance while preserving the rest. Experiments show that StyleStream 2.0 achieves the strongest target style fidelity on VSC, voice design, and voice editing, while remaining competitive on intelligibility and non-edited attribute preservation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Voice style conversion (VSC) modifies how an utterance is spoken while preserving what is said. Following StyleStream 1.0 [42], we define voice style as the joint combination of timbre, accent, and emotion. large body of voice conversion work focuses on timbre conversion, aiming to change speaker identity while preserving content and other paralinguistic factors [52, 37, 61, 9, 4, 41, 65]. Separate lines of work address accent conversion [30, 5, 29] and emotional voice conversion [72, 48, 10] as standalone tasks. More recent systems have begun to address holistic style transfer, jointly converting timbre, accent, and emotion from single reference utterance [69, 36, 68, 3, 42]. Among them, StyleStream 1.0 [42] is the first to demonstrate high-quality zero-shot VSC in streaming setting. However, its approximately one-second end-to-end latency on consumer hardware remains high for latency-sensitive interaction. Reducing this latency while preserving holistic conversion quality is therefore key challenge for making streaming VSC practical. second limitation is that existing VSC systems largely require target reference utterance. This makes voice specification indirect: users must provide an example voice rather than describe the desired attributes. In contrast, text-prompted control has become increasingly common in text-tospeech, where natural-language prompts can specify accent, emotion, and fine-grained vocal qualities such as soft, warm, breathy, or singing-like voice [21, 34, 64, 59, 25, 26, 6, 12]. However, these systems synthesize speech from text rather than converting an input utterance, and therefore do 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). not directly solve streaming speech-to-speech VSC. Recent speech-to-speech conversion work also explores text-guided editing [54, 22, 66, 51], but typically over single axis such as timbre or emotion. To our knowledge, no prior system provides text-based voice design and editing for holistic VSC, let alone in streaming setting. We present StyleStream 2.0, fast and controllable streaming VSC framework that addresses both limitations. StyleStream 2.0 inherits the two-stage architecture of StyleStream 1.0: Destylizer that extracts content features disentangled from style, and Stylizer that reconstructs target speech from those content features and target style. Because StyleStream 1.0 already established the Destylizer as strong content-style disentangler, we reuse it without modification and focus our changes on the Stylizer. To reduce latency, we train few-step pixel MeanFlow [18] Stylizer to replace the multi-step diffusion Stylizer used in StyleStream 1.0. We further fine-tune this Stylizer with autoregressive feedback inspired by Self Forcing [27] to improve robustness under chunk-by-chunk inference. This reduces end-to-end latency to 520 ms on consumer GPU, 2 speedup over StyleStream 1.0, while maintaining conversion quality. To enable text-based control, we change how style enters the Stylizer. StyleStream 1.0 conditions the Stylizer on both an unmasked mel-spectrogram context and style embedding extracted from the target utterance, which leaves style information partially distributed across two conditioning channels. We remove the mel-spectrogram context so that target style is represented through single style embedding. This makes text-based design and editing problem of predicting or modifying this embedding. Inspired by the unified image generation and editing model FLUX Kontext [33], we train unified text-conditioned DiT in the style-embedding space: given natural-language prompt, the model predicts target style embedding for voice design; given an existing utterance embedding and text instruction, the same model modifies the embedding along the requested attribute for voice editing. For text-based control, we focus on age, gender, accent, and emotion. These attributes provide structured and measurable interface for specifying target voices, while covering the major perceptual factors needed for holistic VSC. This structured interface supports both prompt-based voice design and attribute-targeted voice editing, and remains largely unexplored for holistic VSC, especially under streaming constraints. We evaluate StyleStream 2.0 in two settings. First, for standard target-speech-conditioned VSC, we compare against existing reference-based conversion systems and measure conversion quality, intelligibility, and target style fidelity. Second, for text-based control, no native holistic VSC baseline exists. We therefore construct strong cascaded baselines: for voice design, we combine ASR with prompt-controlled TTS; for voice editing, we combine prompt-controlled TTS with reference-based VSC. These cascades benefit from powerful ASR and TTS systems, yet StyleStream 2.0 achieves stronger results on many metrics while remaining pure speech-to-speech system that also supports streaming inference. In summary, our contributions are: We introduce faster streaming VSC model by training few-step pixel MeanFlow Stylizer and fine-tuning it with autoregressive feedback, reducing end-to-end latency to approximately 520 ms on consumer hardware while preserving conversion quality. We propose unified text-conditioned style-embedding model for natural-language voice design and attribute-targeted editing over age, gender, accent, and emotion in holistic VSC. We evaluate StyleStream 2.0 across standard target-speech-conditioned VSC and text-based voice design / editing, showing strong target-style fidelity while remaining competitive in intelligibility, non-edited attribute preservation, and audio quality against both referencebased and cascaded baselines.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Prior speech-to-speech conversion work spans several directions, including voice conversion that primarily changes speaker identity while preserving content and other style factors [52, 37, 61, 9, 4, 40, 32], streaming or real-time voice conversion [41, 65, 45, 63], and separate lines on accent 2 conversion and emotional voice conversion [30, 5, 29, 72, 48, 10]. More recent systems have begun to model richer, holistic voice style across timbre, accent, and emotion, including the Vevo family [69, 36, 68] and StyleStream 1.0 [42]. In parallel, prompt-controlled TTS systems enable naturallanguage specification of target voice characteristics [21, 34, 64, 59, 25, 26, 6, 12], with only few open-source systems explicitly supporting holistic control over timbre, accent, and emotion [60, 25]. Closer to our setting, smaller body of work explores text-guided speech-to-speech conversion [54, 22, 66, 51], but these methods typically focus on single attribute and are evaluated offline. Thus, while prior work shows that speech-to-speech conversion, prompt-based control, and limited text-guided editing are all feasible, no prior system simultaneously provides fast streaming holistic VSC together with unified text-based voice design and editing. Separately, diffusion and flow-matching models have become strong acoustic generators for speech synthesis and conversion [13, 14, 8, 15, 35, 40], but their iterative sampling cost is bottleneck for streaming applications. Recent few-step generative models reduce this cost by producing high-quality samples in only few steps, or even one step [17, 57, 56, 18, 19, 44]. However, fast sampling alone does not guarantee high-quality streaming inference, since short chunks provide limited context and can lead to degraded quality at chunk boundaries. Inspired by Self Forcing for autoregressive video diffusion [27], StyleStream 2.0 combines few-step pixel MeanFlow Stylizer with autoregressive fine-tuning to improve streaming robustness while also enabling controllable holistic voice design and editing.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: StyleStream 2.0 follows the Destylizer-Stylizer framework of StyleStream 1.0 [42]. The Destylizer extracts source content features while suppressing speaker timbre, accent, and emotion. The Stylizer maps these content features and target style embedding to mel-spectrogram, which is converted to waveform by causal Vocos-based vocoder [55]. The style embedding can be obtained from reference utterance or from text-conditioned Voice Controller, allowing the same Stylizer to support reference-based conversion, text-based design, and text-guided editing. We first recap the Destylizer, then introduce the redesigned Stylizer with pixel MeanFlow training and autoregressive feedback fine-tuning, and finally present the Voice Controller for unified voice design and editing. 3.1 Destylizer We use the Destylizer from StyleStream 1.0. The Destylizer consists of frozen HuBERT-Large [24] encoder followed by six conformer [20] blocks. During training, the Destylizer output is passed through finite scalar quantization (FSQ) [47] module and then transformer ASR decoder. The conformer blocks and the ASR decoder are jointly optimized with sequence-to-sequence ASR loss. This training setup encourages the representation to preserve linguistic content, while the compact FSQ bottleneck, with codebook size of 45, discourages encoding style cues that are not needed for character prediction. When applied chunk by chunk, each generation step only observes short segment with limited context, making it difficult to produce locally accurate outputs and smooth transitions across chunk boundaries. Inspired by Self Forcing [27], we apply autoregressive finetuning to adapt the Stylizer to the streaming setting and align training with inference behavior. During this stage, we freeze the style encoder and update only the Stylizer, so the offline and streaming models remain aligned in the same style embedding space. The model rolls out chunks sequentially, maintaining fixed-length window of generated mel frames as past context mpast. Each chunk also receives fixed-size lookahead window of future content features, which provides limited future linguistic context while preserving the streaming constraint. In this work, both tasks focus on controllable age, gender, accent, and emotion. As shown in Figure 1, the Voice Controller is standard DiT trained with JiT-style x-prediction objective over the style-embedding space. Given target style embedding, we add noise to obtain et, patchify it into token sequence, and feed these tokens to the DiT. To unify voice design and editing, we provide an auxiliary embedding sequence with the same patch layout: for voice design, this auxiliary input is learned null embedding; for voice editing, it is the patchified source style embedding. The noised target tokens and auxiliary tokens are concatenated along the channel dimension at each patch. The text prompt is encoded by frozen Flan-T5 encoder2 [11] and injected through cross-attention. For more implementation details, please refer to Appendix B.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: 4.1 Datasets 4.1.1 Voice Style Conversion Training Data. The Destylizer is reused from StyleStream 1.0 without retraining. We train the Stylizer on the English portion of Emilia [23], which provides roughly 50k hours of in-the-wild English speech covering diverse speakers, accents, and emotions. Test Data. We follow the same construction procedure as StyleStream 1.0. We sample 300 source utterances from ESD [71], GLOBE-test [62], and LibriTTS-test-clean [67], and select 10 target utterances from ESD [71], RAVDESS [43], GLOBE-test, and L2-ARCTIC [70], covering five emotions (happy, angry, sad, fearful, calm) and five accents (British, American, Indian, Arabic, Mandarin). Pairing each source with each target yields 3000 source-target pairs. 4.1.2 Voice Design and Editing Training Data. The Voice Controller is trained on large synthetic and natural corpus derived from CapSpeech [60]. We assign four controllable attributes: age, gender, accent, and emotion, using style information from CapSpeech captions, with VoxProfile [16] predictions used as fallbacks when caption labels are missing or ambiguous. To construct single-attribute editing pairs, we use CosyVoice3 [14] to align utterances into shared timbre space for accent and emotion edits: accentedit pairs differ primarily in accent while sharing emotion, and emotion-edit pairs differ primarily in emotion while sharing accent. For timbre editing, we use natural CapSpeech pairs selected to differ in age, gender, or both while preserving the remaining available labels. Categorical labels are converted into natural-language supervision through controlled template renderer, producing prompts for voice design and single-attribute instructions for voice editing. Full details of the label inventories, template construction, and dataset sizes are provided in Appendix A.1. Test Data. We evaluate text-based style control on the same fixed set of 300 source utterances used in Section 4.1.1. For reference-conditioned VSC, we compare against CosyVoice 2.0 [13], CosyVoice 3.0 [14], Vevo [69], Vevo 2.0 [68], and StyleStream 1.0 [42]. We evaluate CosyVoice in its speech-to-speech mode and run Vevo 2.0 as an ASR+TTS cascade using Whisper-large-v3 [53], since Vevo 2.0 is architecturally TTS system. StyleStream 2.0 is evaluated in both offline and streaming modes. Sampling, NFE, CFG, chunk-size, and streaming-buffer details are given in Appendix A.3. Voice Design and Editing. For text-based voice design, we compare against ASR+prompt-TTS cascades using CapTTS [60] and Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign [25]. For text-based voice editing, no native holistic text-editing baseline exists, so we use CapTTS as text-to-reference adapter for Vevo [69] and Vevo 2.0 [68]. The generated reference is routed as either the timbre or style reference depending on the edited attribute. Full routing details are provided in Appendix A.3. 4.3 Metrics Voice Style Conversion. Following StyleStream 1.0 [42], we evaluate reference-conditioned VSC with WER for intelligibility and embedding-based target-style similarity: S-SIM for speaker similarity, A-SIM [73] for accent similarity, and E-SIM [46] for emotion similarity. Subjective evaluation reports NMOS for naturalness and S/A/E-SMOS for speaker, accent, and emotion similarity to the target reference. Voice Design and Editing. For text-based control, we report WER and target-style accuracy using VoxProfile [16] classifiers for age, gender, accent, and emotion, denoted Age-acc, G-acc, A-acc, and E-acc. For voice editing, we additionally measure preservation of non-edited speaker, accent, and emotion attributes using source-output S-SIM, A-SIM, and E-SIM, denoted as S-pres, A-pres, and E-pres. Subjective evaluation reports NMOS for naturalness, SC-MOS for prompt or instruction consistency, and SP-MOS for preservation in editing. Objective metric details and MOS protocols are provided in Appendices A.4 and A.5.

sections.title: 5.3 Voice Design and Editing
sections.content: Table 3 summarizes the voice design results. Compared with the cascaded ASR+TTS baselines, StyleStream 2.0 achieves the strongest overall style fidelity, obtaining the highest style accuracy for age, gender, and accent. The streaming variant also improves over the baselines on age and gender accuracy. CapTTS remains competitive for accent control, while Qwen3-TTS achieves the best intelligibility and emotion accuracy, but shows much lower accent accuracy. Table 4 reports the voice editing results. StyleStream 2.0 offline achieves the highest edited-axis accuracy and the lowest WER, while also receiving the highest naturalness and style-consistency MOS. The streaming variant remains close in both style accuracy and SC-MOS, showing that StyleStream 2.0 can follow edit instructions reliably across different style attributes in both offline and streaming settings. In contrast, Vevo and Vevo 2 obtain lower edited-axis accuracy, especially for accent and emotion edits. Their higher preservation scores therefore should be interpreted together with their lower edit success: in many cases, the source style is preserved because the requested attribute is not changed sufficiently. This highlights the trade-off between successful attribute editing and preservation of unedited attributes. 5.4 Ablation Studies Table 5 reports two ablations on the key design choices of StyleStream 2.0: the autoregressive finetuning (Section 3.2.3) and the perceiver-resampler style encoder (Section 3.2). Without self-forcing, the streaming Stylizer loses substantial intelligibility while target-style similarity stays essentially unchanged, indicating that the autoregressive rollout primarily addresses the train-test mismatch of chunk-by-chunk inference for smooth chunk transitions. Replacing our perceiver-resampler with the StyleStream 1.0 TDNN style encoder under the same offline pMF objective degrades both intelligibility and accent similarity, supporting the need for stronger style encoder when the embedding alone must carry timbre, accent, and emotion. More ablations on the effect of NFE and CFG scale are in Appendix C. Model-size details and Voice Controller text-encoder ablations are in Appendices and C.3.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced StyleStream 2.0, fast and controllable streaming VSC system. By combining few-step pixel MeanFlow Stylizer with autoregressive fine-tuning, it reduces streaming latency while preserving holistic style conversion quality. unified text-conditioned controller further enables natural-language voice design and single-attribute voice editing in the same style-embedding space. Across reference-conditioned VSC, voice design, and editing, StyleStream 2.0 improves target-style fidelity while remaining competitive in intelligibility and preservation.

sections.title: A Extended Data Generation and Evaluation Details
sections.content: This appendix gives additional details for the data generation and evaluation protocol used in the StyleStream 2.0 experiments. We describe the text-based style-control corpus, evaluation manifests, baseline routing for reference-conditioned VSC and text-based control, and objective metrics. A.1 Training Corpus for Text-Based Style Control The main text summarizes the CapSpeech-derived supervised corpus used to train the text-conditioned style-control model. The construction proceeds in four steps: extract candidate attributes from captions and waveforms, normalize and filter those attributes with confidence rules, form nested utterance inventories, and finally sample sourcetarget pairs whose text supervision is rendered from templates. Synthesized portions of the corpus were generated with CosyVoice3 [14] and stored as 24 kHz mono PCM audio. Caption-attribute extraction. CapSpeech captions contain useful natural-language descriptions of speaker attributes, but the descriptions are not normalized into the evaluation taxonomy. We therefore first extract explicit caption attributes with gpt-oss-20b [1]. The model is instructed to copy the captions own wording for accent and emotion rather than normalizing them, so that normalization can be performed by separate deterministic mapping. The extraction prompt used structured function call with fields for age, sex, accent, and emotion: You are given short description of speakers voice. Extract ONLY the attributes the description explicitly states: - age (e.g. young, middle-aged, elderly) - sex (male / female) - accent (regional / national / dialect speech descriptor) - emotion (affective tone) Rules: 1. Copy the descriptions own words VERBATIM for accent and emotion. Do not normalize, translate, bucket, or map them (e.g. if the description says Italian accent, return Italian, NOT Romance; if it says slightly irritated, return slightly irritated, not Anger). 2. Return the literal string N/A for any attribute the description does not mention. Do not infer or guess from unrelated cues. 3. Voice-quality words like deep, raspy, melodic, silky, husky, booming are NOT emotions -- return N/A for emotion unless an actual affective tone is stated. 4. Call the extract_speaker_attributes tool exactly once with the four fields filled in. Output nothing else. The function schema required four string fields. Age was copied when stated, sex was mapped to male/female when explicit, and accent and emotion were copied verbatim from the caption; any missing attribute was returned as N/A. Waveform-profile extraction. Caption attributes are sparse, especially for accent and emotion, so we also run VoxProfile [16] on each CapSpeech utterance. VoxProfile provides an age prediction and posterior distributions for sex, accent, and emotion. These waveform-derived predictions are not used blindly; they serve as fallback labels only when the caption does not provide trusted value. Label normalization and confidence. The extracted caption strings are mapped into the training taxonomy with deterministic normalization rules. Age is bucketed into child [10,15), teen [15,20), young adult [20,35), middle aged [35,55), and old [55,90). Sex labels are male/female. The accent vocabulary is North America, British, Scottish, Northern Irish, Irish, Welsh, Oceania, South African, South Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, Romance, Germanic, Slavic, Semitic, African, and Nordic. The emotion vocabulary is Happiness, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Disgust, Surprise, Neutral, Calm, Friendly, and Authoritative; Contempt is dropped from the final training vocabulary due to lack of samples. Caption labels that normalize to first-class bucket take precedence. When caption label is missing or cannot be mapped, VoxProfile is used only if it passes the confidence threshold for that attribute. Sex fallback requires maximum posterior probability at least 0.99. Accent fallback requires maximum posterior probability at least 0.8 and margin at least 0.4. Emotion fallback requires maximum posterior probability at least 0.7 and margin at least 0.35. Source utterances are further constrained to 220 seconds and predicted age in [10, 90]. Attribute inventories. After normalization, we build three nested inventories from CapSpeech utterances. The broadest inventory, Ivc, contains utterances with confident age and sex labels and is used as pool of target voice prompts for voice conversion. The generation inventory, Igen, additionally requires either an accent or an emotion label. The editing inventory, Ied, requires all four labels: age, sex, accent, and emotion. The final inventory sizes are 496,954 rows for Ivc, 403,013 rows for Igen, and 59,613 rows for Ied. Pair sampling and training tiers. Training examples are sampled from the inventories after the label taxonomy and inventory filters are fixed. For voice design, source utterance from Igen is converted using target speaker from Ivc. The content is held fixed while the target profile specifies either age, sex, and accent, or age, sex, and emotion. For accent editing, source and target utterances share the same emotion but differ in accent; both sides are re-voiced with shared timbre so that accent is the intended changing factor. For emotion editing, source and target utterances share the same accent but differ in emotion. For timbre editing, pairs are natural recordings selected to differ in age, sex, or both while preserving the other available labels. Table 6 summarizes the produced training tiers. Table 6: Training tiers for the text-based StyleStream 2.0 corpus. Tier Samples Audio source Voice design Accent editing Emotion editing Age editing Gender editing Joint age+gender editing Synthesized Synthesized Synthesized 2,000,005 3,000,028 2,999,992 1,499,961 Natural 1,481,314 Natural 1,000,001 Natural Total 11.98M Template generation and rendering. Each sampled example is rendered into voice-design prompt or edit instruction using shared template inventory. We generated this inventory with gptoss-120b [1] by providing hand-written seed templates for each template shape and asking for diverse paraphrases that preserve fixed set of placeholders. The template shapes were: all-attribute design, timbre+accent design, timbre+emotion design, age editing, gender editing, joint age+gender editing, accent editing, and emotion editing. The total inventory contains approximately 9000 generated phrasings plus attribute surface-form expansions such as American for North America and Australian or New Zealand for Oceania. The template-generation prompt was: You generate caption templates for text-to-speech dataset. Shape: <shape name> Each template MUST contain exactly these placeholders, each used exactly once: <placeholder list>. No other placeholders. Do not expand the placeholders into words. Keep each template to one natural-sounding English sentence, under 25 words. Vary sentence structure, word choice, and phrasing. Here are <N> seed templates for reference: 1. <seed template 1> 2. <seed template 2> ... Produce <K> NEW templates, distinct from the seeds and from each other. For example, an all-attribute design template required the placeholders {age}, {gender}, {accent}, and {emotion}, while an accent-editing instruction required only {tgt_accent}. Generated templates were filtered to require every specified placeholder exactly once, reject unknown placeholders, and limit the length of each sentence. A.2 Text-Based Evaluation Manifests The main text describes the 300-source, 3000-design-item, and 3000-edit-item evaluation setup. The source set contains 50 utterances from ESD, 100 from GLOBE, and 150 from LibriTTS. Below we report the source-label distribution and target-sampling details that are not shown in the main text. Evaluation task structure. All text-based evaluations use the same fixed 300 source utterances as the reference-conditioned VSC evaluation. The voice-design manifest contains 3000 items, formed by pairing each source with ten style prompts. The voice-editing manifest also contains 3000 items, formed by pairing each source with ten single-axis edit instructions: two age edits, two gender edits, three accent edits, and three emotion edits. For each edit, the target value is sampled to differ from the source label on the edited axis, and the instruction text mentions only the edited attribute. Evaluation prompts and edit instructions are rendered with the same controlled template renderer used for training. Voice design mix. Table 7 gives the fixed prompt mix. The instruction text mentions only the edited attribute; it does not contain explicit preserve clauses. A.3 Systems and Baseline Generation The main text lists the compared systems. Here we give the routing details that are easy to omit from the compact experimental setup. Reference-conditioned VSC systems. For reference-conditioned VSC, we compare against CosyVoice 2.0 [13], CosyVoice 3.0 [14], Vevo [69], Vevo 2.0 [68], and StyleStream 1.0 [42]. We use the CosyVoice 2.0 and CosyVoice 3.0 flow-matching speech-to-speech usage. Vevo 2.0 is run as an ASR+TTS cascade: Whisper-large-v3 [53] transcribes the source and target utterances, and the transcripts together with the target waveform are fed to Vevo 2.0 to synthesize the output. All systems are evaluated with the standard Euler sampler. Baseline NFEs follow each systems recommended setting when applicable: 32 for Vevo and Vevo 2.0, 10 for the CosyVoice variants, and 16 for StyleStream 1.0 offline. Qwen3-TTS [25] is additionally evaluated as an offline Whisper-large-v3 + voice-cloning TTS cascade, using the source transcript and target reference speech. Streaming inference settings. StyleStream 2.0 uses 4 function evaluations (NFE) and fixed CFG guidance scale ω = 3 in both offline and streaming modes. The main streaming configuration uses 300 ms chunk size and an 80 ms lookahead. During streaming inference, we maintain two 3-second ring buffers: content ring buffer and past self-generated mel-context ring buffer. For streaming baselines, we use the largest NFE that satisfies the real-time per-chunk budget on RTX 4060; this gives 12 NFE for StyleStream 1.0 streaming at 600 ms chunk size. Vocoder and timing. We use the same causal Vocos-based streaming vocoder as StyleStream 1.0 [42, 55]. Processing times include mel generation and vocoder inference through waveform output; the vocoder contributes approximately 3.139 ms per 300 ms chunk, already included in the reported 140.7 ms processing time. Design systems. For CapTTS [60] and Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign [25], the source utterance is first transcribed with Whisper-large-v3 [53]; the baseline receives this ASR transcript plus the design prompt. The known source transcript is reserved for WER evaluation. Editing systems. The editing baselines are Vevo [69] and Vevo2 [68], using the Amphion implementations [36]. For each edit row, CapTTS first generates target reference WAV using the post-edit target labels rendered through the same template family and random Whisper transcript from the source transcript pool. This reference provides the requested target style or timbre to Vevo/Vevo2. For Vevo, we use the Vevo-Style for all text-based editing. For age or gender edits, the CapTTS reference is used as the timbre reference and the original source is used as the style reference. For accent or emotion edits, the original source is used as the timbre reference and the CapTTS reference is used as the style reference. For Vevo2, the source utterance is transcribed with Whisper to form Tsrc, and the CapTTS reference is transcribed with Whisper to form Ttgt. For age or gender edits, Vevo2 receives the source style reference with Tsrc and the CapTTS timbre reference. For accent or emotion edits, Vevo2 receives the CapTTS style reference with Ttgt and the source timbre reference. In all cases, the target text for the output is Tsrc. A.4 Objective Evaluation Details Similarity models. S-SIM is computed with Resemblyzer3, A-SIM with the CommonAccent ECAPA model4 [73], and E-SIM with emotion2vec5 [46]. For reference-conditioned VSC, similarities are computed between the converted utterance and the target reference. For editing, similarities are computed between the source utterance and the generated edit output. checkpoints [16] age/sex, VoxProfile classifiers. The main text defines The VoxProfile scoring tiantiaf/wavlm-large-age-sex and for tiantiaf/whisper-large-v3-msp-podcast-emotion for emotion. Generated audio is downmixed to mono, resampled to 16 kHz, and truncated to 15 seconds before inference. Age predictions are collapsed into young, middle-aged. the attribute accuracies. are tiantiaf/wavlm-large-narrow-accent accent, used for for WER and similarity. WER is computed by transcribing generated audio with Whisper-largev3 [53] and comparing against the known source transcript, not against the Whisper transcript used to drive cascaded baselines. For editing, S-SIM, A-SIM, and E-SIM are computed between the source utterance and the generated edit output. Each similarity is split according to whether the corresponding factor should be preserved or changed by the instruction; preservation scores are better when higher, while change scores are better when lower. A.5 Subjective Evaluation Protocol Recruitment and screening. All subjective evaluations are deployed on Prolific6. We recruit 40 participants. We restrict participation to listeners whose first language is English and who report fluent English proficiency, with Prolific approval rating of at least 95%. Submissions completed faster than the expected minimum task duration are automatically rejected to filter low-effort responses, 3https://github.com/resemble-ai/Resemblyzer 4https://huggingface.co/Jzuluaga/accent-id-commonaccentecapa 5https://github.com/ddlBoJack/emotion2vec 6https://www.prolific.com 18 and listeners are encouraged to take the survey on laptop or desktop with headphones for the best audio experience. Survey types. We deploy four types of subjective surveys, all using 5-point integer scale: NMOS for naturalness (90 items per survey); SMOS for style similarity, in three variants: S-SMOS (speaker), A-SMOS (accent), E-SMOS (emotion), with 80 paired items per variant; voice-design (VD) for text-prompted voice design (40 items per survey); and voice-editing (VE) for instruction-based voice editing (40 items per survey). Representative survey interfaces are shown in Figures 2 and 3. We compensate participants at rate of at least $20 per hour. The NMOS studies take approximately 10 minutes on average, corresponding to $3.50 per participant. The SMOS studies take approximately 20 minutes on average, corresponding to $7.00 per participant. The voice design and voice editing studies take approximately 10 minutes on average, corresponding to $3.50 per participant. NMOS. Listeners rate the naturalness of single test audio sample on 5-point scale (1: completely unnatural, 5: completely natural), guided by the question Do they sound like real humans?. SMOS (speaker, accent, emotion). For each SMOS survey, listeners are presented with Test and Target audio pair, and rate similarity along the indicated style axis on 5-point scale (1: not similar at all, 5: very similar). S-SMOS rates speaker timbre, A-SMOS rates accent, and E-SMOS rates emotion. Listeners are explicitly instructed to focus only on the indicated axis and to ignore the other style axes as well as recording-quality differences. Voice design (VD). Each item pairs Source recording with Test audio (the models attempt to re-render the source content in the prompted style), accompanied by natural-language style prompt (e.g., Hear young adult guy articulate words with British accent.). Listeners give two 5-point ratings: naturalness, and style match against the prompt. The question text on each page lists exactly which prompt-mentioned attributes the listener should focus on for the style-match rating. Voice editing (VE). Each item pairs Source recording with Test audio (the source after the requested edit), accompanied by natural-language edit instruction (e.g., Produce an older person sounding output.). Listeners give three 5-point ratings: naturalness, edit match (does the test apply the instruction correctly?), and preservation (does the test keep the non-edited attributes the same as the source?). The question text on each page lists which attribute is being edited and which attributes should be preserved.

sections.title: B Implementation Details
sections.content: This section reports the full architecture and training configurations of all StyleStream 2.0 components. The Destylizer is reused from StyleStream 1.0 without modification. B.1 Stylizer Architecture. The Stylizer is 16-layer DiT with hidden dimension 768, FFN expansion ratio 4 (FFN dimension 3072), and 12 attention heads. StyleStream 1.0 uses the same 16-layer Stylizer DiT backbone. We use ALiBi positional encoding [50] and adaLN-Zero conditioning [49] driven by the summed embedding of (r, t, es, ω). At the input, zt (100 mel bins), fc (768-dimensional content features), and the past-mel-context channel (100 mel bins, zeroed during offline training) are concatenated along the channel dimension and projected to the hidden size. The output is 100-channel x-prediction of the target mel-spectrogram, from which the average velocity uθ and the implied instantaneous velocity Vθ are computed as in 3.2. Style encoder. The style encoder uses frozen microsoft/wavlm-base-plus backbone, with the outputs of all 12 transformer layers concatenated along the time axis as in 3.2. The perceiverresampler stacks 4 blocks; each block first cross-attends from Nq = 8 learnable queries (query dimension 128) to the WavLM features, then self-attends among the queries, with 4 attention heads in both stages. The flattened pooled representation of size Nq 128 = 1024 is mapped through an MLP to the output style embedding es RC with = 768. Including the frozen speech backbone, the StyleStream 2.0 style encoder has 97.5M parameters compared with 128.4M for StyleStream 1.0. 19 (a) NMOS (b) E-SMOS Figure 2: Naturalness MOS (NMOS) and Emotion SMOS (E-SMOS) evaluation interfaces. The S-SMOS and A-SMOS surveys are analogous to E-SMOS, with the emotion target replaced by speaker identity or accent and the listener instructed to ignore the other style axes. Mel-spectrogram and audio configuration. Audio is sampled at 16 kHz and converted to 100-bin mel-spectrograms at 50 Hz frame rate, matching the Destylizer output rate. Training uses 6-second segments. Offline pMF training. The Stylizer is trained from scratch on Emilia-EN with the pMF objective. For each training utterance we sample and with = on 75% of training samples (a pure flowmatching step, where the loss reduces to direct supervision of the instantaneous velocity) and < on the remaining 25% (a MeanFlow average-velocity step, with the total derivative in Vθ computed via JVP). The diffusion time is sampled as logitnormal distribution = σ(ℓ) with ℓ (Pmean, 2 std) and Pmean = Pstd = 0.8, and replaced with U[0, 1] on 10% of training samples. Here σ() is the sigmoid function. The guidance scale is sampled as ω = (1 + ωmax)u with U[0, 1] and ωmax = 7, equivalent to log-uniform sampling on [1, 1 + ωmax]. We drop the condition = (fc, es) with probability pdrop = 0.2, replacing it with . We optimize with AdamW at peak learning rate 104, weight decay 106, 2000 warmup steps and cosine decay to 106, in bf16-mixed precision, for 1M steps with global batch size of 256 on 8 H100 GPUs. Autoregressive fine-tuning. We initialize from the offline pMF checkpoint and fine-tune with the Self Forcing chunked rollout while keeping the pMF objective; the FM / MeanFlow split is shifted to 90% / 10% so that most fine-tuning steps are pure flow-matching. The sampling, ω sampling, and conditioning dropout follow the offline stage. Each rollout uses one ODE step per chunk with fixed rollout-time guidance scale ωrollout = 3. For each batch we randomly sample the chunk size {8, . . . , 30} frames (160 to 600 ms at 50 Hz), and use 3-second prefix and 3-second past-context window (150 frames each at 50 Hz). The training loss is computed only on the current chunk region. We optimize with AdamW at peak learning rate 104, weight decay 106, 1000 warmup steps and cosine decay to 106, in bf16-mixed precision, for 400k steps with global batch size of 64 on 32 H100 GPUs. B.2 Voice Controller Architecture. The Voice Controller is standard 16-layer DiT with hidden dimension 1024, FFN expansion ratio 4 (FFN dimension 4096), and 16 attention heads, using RoPE positional encoding [58]. It is an additional module for text-based design/editing and is not involved in reference-conditioned 20 (a) Voice design (VD) (b) Voice editing (VE) Figure 3: Voice-design (VD) and voice-editing (VE) evaluation interfaces. Each item pairs source and test audio sample with natural-language style prompt (VD) or edit instruction (VE), and asks for naturalness plus task-specific match (and preservation, for VE) ratings. VSC. The text prompt is encoded by frozen Flan-T5 base7 and injected via cross-attention. The model operates on style embeddings of dimension = 768. We patchify the noised embedding et with patch size = 32 into C/P = 24 tokens of dimension 32, and concatenate them channelwise with an auxiliary input of the same shape (a learned null embedding for voice design, the patchified source style embedding for voice editing) before projecting to the hidden dimension. Style embeddings are normalized using the global training-set mean and standard deviation during training, and de-normalized at inference. Training. We train the Voice Controller jointly on voice design and voice editing with the xprediction flow-matching objective, splitting each mini-batch evenly between the two tasks. The diffusion time is sampled from the same logit-normal distribution as the Stylizer (B.1), = σ(ℓ) with ℓ (Pmean, 2 std) and Pmean = Pstd = 0.8. We apply standard CFG dropout on the text prompt with probability pdrop = 0.2. We optimize with AdamW at peak learning rate 104, weight decay 106, 1000 warmup steps and cosine decay to 3 105, in bf16-mixed precision, for 500k steps with global batch size of 1024 on 8 H100 GPUs. Inference. We sample the target style embedding with the standard two-pass CFG sampler, using NFE = 64 and CFG guidance scale ω = 4. The generated embedding is de-normalized with the stored training-set statistics before being passed to the Stylizer as es. The controller prepares this embedding once before streaming, and it is reused across chunks.

sections.title: E Broader Impacts
sections.content: StyleStream 2.0 enables low-latency, controllable voice style conversion and text-conditioned voice design and editing. Beneficial applications include accessibility tools, voice-based privacy and anonymization, accent localization for media, language-learning aids, and creative audio production. Like other high-quality generative voice systems, StyleStream 2.0 also carries risks of misuse, particularly for voice impersonation, fraud, or synthetic disinformation. Our training data comes entirely from existing publicly released speech corpora, with no additional scraping of identifiable individuals. As safeguards for responsible release, we plan to release model weights under license that prohibits impersonation and other malicious applications, accompanied by model card documenting training data, intended uses, and known biases, and we support continued research on synthetic-speech detection and audio watermarking.
